justifications.c1: Many independent per-incident losses well above £5k (Telegraph £400k, Leamington £80k, Express & Star £75k, Grimsby £40k, Durham £22k) plus capped payouts of £7.5k–£10k; but because theft is rare per church, payback within 12 months for a typical site is not shown.
justifications.c2: Theft is rare per site: ~58 recorded lead/metal thefts a year nationally (Countryside Alliance FOI via Church Times) across thousands of churches; repeat targeting is anecdotal; no monthly or weekly check duty was found (researcher records 'not found'), only annual maintenance.
justifications.c3: Paid workaround quantified by credible non-vendor sources: £3–5k approved alarm purchase plus annual maintenance (Diocese of Oxford, search-confirmed), ~£600/yr running costs (OHCT enrolment form), extra first-responder fees (Ely guidance).
justifications.c4: Named insurer condition: Ecclesiastical requires an approved, monitored roof alarm for vulnerable churches to get increased cover (search-confirmed), Electronic Protection Condition, with capped payouts in practice (£7.5k, £10k) and a claim refusal noted by Law & Religion UK.
justifications.c5: PCCs and churchwardens are evidenced as the commissioning body (diocesan guidance, PCC minutes), but they are volunteer committees that depend on grants (Benefact Trust up to £2,500) and need faculty permission, so budget is fragmented.
justifications.c6: Ecclesiastical's approved roof-alarm supplier list and county-trust bulk schemes with named installers (OHCT/E-Bound, Norfolk PCC partnership) already sell exactly this; but a new entrant must win insurer approval to use them.
justifications.c7: Willingness to pay is proven (£3–5k plus ~£600/yr, grants), but incumbents (E-Bound, Ace Defence, i4S) serve the niche and the PSTN problem is already met by commodity 4G communicators (CSL, Pyronix); the researcher found no PSTN pain specific to churches.
justifications.c8: The only priced sensor (Milesight WS202, ~£52) is IP30 indoor-only; an outdoor roof version, insurer approved-supplier performance standard, Historic England consultation and bird-triggered false alarms (Wokingham fabric report) all add risk.
justifications.c9: Insurer condition requires the alarm to be active and monitored at the time of theft (Ely, search-confirmed), grants require a 5-year maintenance commitment, and existing schemes charge ~£600/yr.
justifications.c10: Diocesan statements, police FOI data via Countryside Alliance/Church Times, insurance trade press (Post), many local news reports and parish fabric reports; no forum-style first-hand complaints.

weakest: Lead theft is a rare event per church (around 58 recorded thefts a year nationally) with no monthly check duty, so value cannot be shown in a 1–3-month pilot, and the PSTN pain is not evidenced for churches at all.
